title: What is known about 1RB1RF_1RC0LD_1LB1RA_1RE1LE_0RC0LB_0RB---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RF_1RC0LD_1LB1RA_1RE1LE_0RC0LB_0RB---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The run is understood at the level of passes: the tape is a run of 1s with a few 0s; one 0 (the marker) moves right by 4 cells per bounce while the right end moves by 1, so a marker that starts g cells from the end catches it after about g/3 bounces and the pass ends with the tape g/3 cells wider. New markers start near the left end, so the width is multiplied by about 4/3 per pass (checked for the 21 passes to 1.6·1010 steps). Which marker comes next is decided by a short prefix at the left end and by residues of the width mod 3; whether that Collatz-like process ever lines up to halt is not known.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 48,668 cells have been visited and 34,210 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.151). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.516).

claims.title: Shift rules of the sweeps
claims.text: The two sweeps are shift rules: to the right the head turns each triple 100, 001 or 010 (by its phase) into 111, to the left it turns 111 back into 001, 100 or 010; and one bounce of the marker zig-zag, L 0 1 1 (111)^(m+1) D>1 0^∞ → L 1111 0 11 (111)^m 1 B>1 1 0^∞ (the marker 4 cells to the right, the gap to the end 2 shorter), for every m and every tape L.

claims.title: No halt in the first 2·10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: c/passes.c (the plain simulator of tools/c/tm.h, printing the passes of the marker) runs 2·1010 steps without a halt; the last pass that ends in that range ends at step 15,689,894,237 with the tape 192,218 cells wide.

claims.title: The marker zig-zag
claims.text: Between passes the head bounces between the marker (a single 0 in a run of 1s) and the right end. Two bounces take L 0 (111)^(m+2) B>1 0^∞ to L 1^8 0 (111)^m B>1 0^∞; by induction 2j bounces take gap 3(m+2j) to 3m, leaving 1^(8j) behind the marker, for every m, j and every tape L. With the first bounce after a launch at gap ≡ 1 (mod 3), and the launches from the left end with no marker (width ≡ 0 or 2), a pass from gap 3(e+2j+1)+1 reaches gap 3e with the tape 2j cells wider.

claims.title: Growth by 4/3 per pass
claims.text: A pass whose marker starts g cells from the right end ends with the tape g/3 cells wider, up to a few cells (checked on every pass with a single marker to 1.6·10<sup>10</sup> steps). The widths at the ends of passes run 706, 945, 1266, 1694, 2258, 2993, 3971, 5301, 7069, 9410, 12506, 16503, 21553, 28137, 36714, 47058, 60838, 81101, 108115, 144158, 192218: ratios between 1.28 and 1.34. The zig-zag part of this is proved (see above); the end of a pass, the left-end turn with a prefix and the launches with a marker at gap ≡ 0 or 2 (mod 3) are not, so the exact pass map is not yet written.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The run is a Collatz-like process: each pass multiplies the width by about 4/3, and the prefix at the left end, which decides where the next marker starts, changes with the width mod 3 (the leftward sweep converts the tape in triples counted from the right end). The halting transition F1 needs A to read 1 followed by another 1, which happens only if a rightward sweep meets triples that are not in the phase it expects; nobody has shown that the residues never produce that.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine keeps a run of 1s with a few 0s in it. One 0, the marker, creeps to the right end of the tape while the head bounces between it and the end; each time it arrives the tape is about a third wider, and a few cells at the left end decide where the next marker starts. That is a Collatz-like map, and whether it ever leads to the one halting pattern is open.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 48,668 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).
No halt in a direct run (c/passes.c).
The width grows by about a third per pass of the marker.

sections.heading: A run of 1s, written two ways
html: Almost every cell of the tape is a 1. The head writes them in two encodings: a sweep to the right turns each triple 100 into 111, and a sweep to the left turns 111 back into 001 (or 100, 010, depending on where in a triple it starts). Both sweeps are proved shift rules (lean/Rules.lean). So the same tape looks like this at the two ends of the run:
In what follows the tape is always read at the right end, in the all-1s encoding: then it is a few blocks of 1s separated by single 0s.

sections.heading: The marker zig-zag
html: Most of the time the head does not cross the whole tape. It bounces between the right end and one 0, the marker, and each bounce moves the marker 4 cells to the right while the end moves 1. Four consecutive right-end turns of the real run:
As a rule on the gap g between the marker and the head:

X 0 1^g B>1 1   →   X 1^4 0 1^(g-4) D>1 0
X 0 1^g D>1 0   →   X 1^4 0 1^(g-2) B>1 1

The second line is a Lean theorem for every g ≡ 2 (mod 3) and every tape X (zig_d); the two lines together, as one double bounce, are z_two, and z_pass runs the whole zig-zag by induction on the gap (lean/Pass.lean). Each bounce costs about 2g steps, so the zig-zag of a marker that starts g cells from the end takes about g²/3 steps.

sections.heading: Each pass makes the tape a third wider
html: The marker gains 3 cells on the end per bounce, so a marker launched g cells from the end needs about g/3 bounces, and meanwhile the end moves g/3 cells. New markers are launched close to the left end, so g is nearly the whole width W, and the pass ends with the width close to 4W/3. The widths at the ends of the passes of the run:

The run to 1.6·1010 steps has 21 passes after the first few hundred steps; the number of steps grows like the square of the width (about 0.42·W²), so the right end of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, and the number of passes only like its logarithm.

sections.heading: The prefix and the residues
html: When a marker reaches the end, the head sweeps back over the whole tape to the left end, changes a few cells there and launches the next marker. The cells left of the new marker form a short prefix, and the run keeps only a handful of shapes for it, for example 1 0, 1 0 1^39 0, 1^73 0, or two old markers left behind, 1^73 0 1^2355 0. Which shape comes next depends on the width modulo 3, because the leftward sweep converts the tape in triples counted from the right end, and its last, incomplete triple is what the head meets at the left end.

The only halting transition is F1: A reads a 1 and F reads the next cell, also a 1 (A>1 1). In a correct sweep A always meets a 0 there; the pattern needs a rightward sweep to meet triples in a phase it does not expect. So the machine is a Collatz-like map, width ×4/3 with a residue-dependent correction and a finite-state prefix, and halting is the question whether its residues ever produce that mismatch. That is open (a heuristic statement of the structure, not a proof of either answer).

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.151). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.516).
After 109 steps the tape spans 48,668 cells (61 left of the start, 35,214 right), with a density of 1s of 0.703.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: A single 0 (a marker) zig-zags between itself and the right end of a run of 1s until it catches the end; each such pass makes the tape about 4/3 times wider, and a short prefix at the left end records the residues: a Collatz-like 4/3 map.
